canonical_topic: Transmission overload risk from correlated wind ramp-up
definition: Wind power is often constrained by limited long-distance transmission capacity, and because turbines in a region tend to start producing together when wind picks up, the shared transmission lines can become congested/overloaded.
core_idea: Remote wind farms depend on costly long-distance transmission lines to reach load; because wind across a region tends to rise simultaneously, all turbines can ramp up output together and overload that shared transmission path, similar to a rush-hour traffic jam limiting how much generation can actually reach consumers.
key_points: Long-distance transmission to remote wind sites is expensive to build and maintain.
Wind output across a region tends to rise together, so many turbines can start producing at the same time.
This simultaneous ramp-up can overload the transmission lines carrying that power to load, creating congestion analogous to rush-hour traffic.
trading_implications: Correlated regional wind ramps can drive transmission congestion, which is a relevant driver of locational basis and congestion cost between a wind-heavy zone and load centers.
Curtailment risk during high-wind periods should be considered when evaluating expected wind output that actually reaches the grid.
caveats: Assuming turbine-level output alone determines delivered power, without accounting for transmission capacity limits.
